utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Now, under the procedure here we have questions asked of you to assist us. Mr. Stamp, I believe, will be asking you some questions to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trajkovic. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please begin by just telling us your name, your father's first name, your date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Zivko Trajkovic, father's name Trajan, born on the 12th of December, 1957, in the village of Strezovce, Kosovska Kamenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand, Mr. Trajkovic, that you are a retired former member of the MUP of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you retire from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In late 2007, in the month of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you give us just a concise history of your role in the MUP over the years from when you joined and the positions you held and where you were based up until the time of your retirement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I began working at the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, which was then the Secretariat of Internal Affairs, in 1982. I reported to work at the secretariat as a police officer for securing the republic organs. I worked this until September 1982, when I applied to work in the special units of the interior ministry. As I passed the test to work in the special units, beginning on September 1st, 1982, I was re-deployed to work within the special units of the Secretariat of the Interior. I completed all the training that was envisaged, and I was promoted in service while at the same time I graduated at the Faculty of National Defence in Belgrade. I worked as a group leader, commander of a squad. I was deputy commander of a unit. I was deputy commander, and I was the commander of a special unit, and from 1992 onwards the special units were renamed and were now called Special Anti-Terrorist Units. Their composition now included the Special Anti-Terrorist Units seated in Pristina as well as the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit seated in Novi Sad as well as the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit seated in Belgrade. Beginning in 1982 I worked with the special units of the Secretariat of the Interior, then later on these were the special units of the Ministry of the Interior, and with them I passed a lot of time in various places in the field, whether for training purposes, and the training was extremely hard and difficult, and we were also in the field in order to carry out the tasks that had to do with anti-terrorist suppression, mostly in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. Beginning in 1981 we had counter-revolution there that was the way it was called in our public, that was the way it was presented to our public, it was a counter-revolution mounted by one part of the Albanian population in Kosovo, with a request that this territory should secede from the Republic of Serbia. The focus of our activities and tasks was the territory of Kosovo, and we also carried out a number of various operations on the territory of Serbia, especially when we had to deal with serious cases of crime, with criminals who could not have been arrested by the ordinary police that carried out everyday tasks. In such situations they always asked for the assistance of our units. Beginning in -- during 1981, beginning on the 21st of September, 1981, and until the end of April I was in the territory of Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem with a group of our members, the members of the special unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, is this 1981 or --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: 1991. In 1991, beginning on the 21st of September, to the end of April 1992, when after having completed the task with the group of our members we returned to our base in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I would just like to move to 1998 and 1999. At that time what position did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 my position was the commander of all special units within the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the organisation known as the SAJ, the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As this abbreviation will be used frequently, I propose that we use the shortened form, SAJ, that means Special Anti-Terrorist Units of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on could I show you very quickly a document, 65 ter 04200, it's P145.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps on the copy in Serbian we could scroll down so we can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately the signature on the Serbian copy is hardly visible. I can just see that this was printed and that this is Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, but the signature is hardly legible at least here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I take it that you had a copy to -- had an opportunity to look at a copy of this. Would this be the official decision terminating your participation in the -- in operations in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that should be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could remove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us a little bit about the purpose of the SAJ. Could you give us some more information about its structure in 1998 and 1999. I think you said that there were three seats: One in Belgrade, one in Novi Sad, and the other in Pristina. Who were the commanders, and how many men did these units or subunits have within their structure?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: All three units were part of the systemisation of the Serbian MUP, and they were based on the main principle. They had a commander, they had a deputy commander, they also had a command, a command of a unit, also the operational segment, then the support section, and the section that secured the centres where the units were located. The commander of the Belgrade SAJ was Mr. Zoran Simovic. The commander of the Novi Sad SAJ was Mr. Branko Curcic. The commander of the Pristina SAJ was Mr. Radoslav Stalevic. All three units according to the systemisation had about 100 men, but their composition was never full. And the operational section numbered together with the command around 60 members, and the rest were the drivers, then the centre security, and the administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were these three units located? Did they have a central place where they maintained barracks or offices? Let's start with the one in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The unit seated in Pristina was quartered near Pristina at a centre. It used to be the Territorial Defence centre for Pristina. And later on the special unit of the then-Pristina Secretariat of the Interior, that is to say the provincial Secretariat of the Interior, was based there. And when in 1991 almost 99 per cent of the ethnic Albanian members left their positions in Kosovo and Metohija, that also affected the special unit. Until 1991 it had a mixed composition. It had members who were both ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanians, but in 1991 the unit was attached to the Joint Command of the Special Anti-Terrorist Units in Belgrade, and since then, since 1991, it was a unit that had its centre in Ajvalija, that was the former Territorial Defence centre. The Special Anti-Terrorist Unit based in Belgrade since its foundation moved from one location to another, there was several locations all in all, for a while they were attached to the department of the interior in new Belgrade. Later on they were quartered at the Belgrade airport in Curcin, where the helicopter and special units were located. And since 1992, late 1992 or 1993, the seat of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit from Belgrade was in Batajnica. It has been in Batajnica at the 13th of May centre near Batajnica. The seat of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit in Novi Sad is near Novi Sad. It is also a Territorial Defence centre, a former one, in a place called Klisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where was your office as the overall command of all three units?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: My offices were in the building of the Ministry of the Interior in Kneza Milosa Street 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 1998, could you tell us what were the main tasks that the SAJ units were engaged in in that year?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1998 our units mainly had the task to assist the branch secretariats of the interior to resolve the mounting problems that had to do with security in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The Novi Sad SAJ and the Pristina SAJ were quartered in the Pristina premises of the SAJ in Ajvalija, and the Belgrade SAJ was sent to the secretariat in Prizren in order to carry out tasks in that region. Our tasks were mostly to resolve the situation as regards to the problems with roads that had been temporarily taken over. That was the Pristina-Pec road, the Pristina-Prizren road, as well as the Prizren-Pec road. It happened that because of the territories that were covered by Albanian terrorists, for long periods these roads were not accessible. It was not possible for normal traffic to move along these roads on the territory of the province of Kosovo. And unblocking these roads was mostly the tasks of our units with the assistance of the members of the special police units. In these areas, police check-points were sometimes mounted in order to secure these roads. I have to note that in this period, I mean the first half of 1998, sometimes we had tasks such as securing police squads that were re-deployed and that were the target of Albanian terrorists; and then on the basis of plans that were prepared by the MUP staff in Pristina our units had the task to secure such police squads as well as some check-points that were the targets of attacks. These were the check-points that I mentioned a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were some of the -- please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: May I just finish, please? One of the more serious operations that we carried out at the time was unblocking the Belacevac mine, as the terrorists had completely taken over this mine, and they unabled the production of electricity in Kosovo A and B plans and that was mostly all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move to the second half of 1998, could you just indicate to us what type of weaponry did these units on your command have at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1998 the weaponry was mostly classical weaponry that the members of the Special Anti-Terrorist Units had, but as the problems became more and more complex, as there were more and more attacks on the check-points and our units which were on the move, then we had to take some measures that meant that we had to armour our field vehicles and that we had to introduce more heavy calibres like 12.7 and also -- and also mortars 60- and 82-millmetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the -- well, on the 5th of March, 1998, there was an assault by members of the MUP forces on the Jashari compound in Drenica. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know which unit plan -- or should I say who planned this operation and which units participated in it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This operation was planned by the operations service of the State Security Service. As for who participated in the operation, it was the unit for special operations as well as the SAJ -- or rather, a part of the Novi Sad SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Pristina SAJ, which was also based in Kosovo at that time, participate?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Two combat teams from the SAJ Pristina and from the SAJ Belgrade took part together with the members of the special police units in the -- in the blockade of that region. This area was notorious for terrorist activities, and the plan was to defend the units who were to arrest Jashari and his group in case there was a terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on, you said that the operation was planned by the operation service of the State Security Service and the participants in the operation included a unit for special operations. Was this unit for special operations also known by its acronym, the JSO?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: JSO stands for Special Operations Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who commanded the units involved in the assault on the Jashari compound?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, Franko Simatovic was the commander of that action. His nickname is Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as some of your units were involved in some way in the action, did you come to your own assessment of the way the operation was handled?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I made an assessment for myself, but since I wasn't involved in the planning of that operation, given that it was a small area, we would normally call that "action" and not "operation." Nobody came to ask me whether I agreed with the proposal that had been advanced by them, and we didn't really have much opportunity to give comments on how that action was to be carried out. But since I had a lot of experience in dealing with such and similar problems, I believed that the action had not been planned well and that it could have been done differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have had evidence before the Court, Mr. Trajkovic, that among the persons killed in this action there were -- well, there were 84 persons killed, including 24 women and children, in this action. Would the leadership of the public security department in Belgrade be aware of the casualties that resulted from this action?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I hear of this figure of 84, and if Mr. Stamp is quoting somebody I would kindly ask him to tell us who he's quoting, and he should put it to the witness. Quite the contrary. I believe that we had different data provided by some witnesses. I think it was Mr. Cvijetic who spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your precise number, 84, is a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see that on this occasion my friend is correct. I should have said 54, and that I think was the evidence of Mr. Fred Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're referring to the killing of 54 people in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I proceed, Your Honour? I'm prepared to rephrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, did you become aware that there were civilian casualties that resulted from the operation? Forget about the numbers now, but that there were in fact civilian casualties that resulted from the operation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that there had been civilian casualties, but as to the figure I wasn't aware of it. I know that there was an on-site investigation, that an investigating judge went to the site, and that the police unit from the regional secretariat assisted in that investigation and that a report was produced immediately after the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would the leadership of the public security department in Belgrade have become aware of the civilian casualties that resulted from this operation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose they did become aware. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- well, from your experience as a senior member of the police where a major operation -- a major action, I beg your pardon, a major action of this nature takes place and there are casualties, would the reports indicate the amount and nature of these casualties, that is, the reports up to the headquarters of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have mentioned that this action was planned by this state [Realtime transcript read in error "date"] security service, and I truly do not know that anybody from the public security department took part in the planning. That is to say that the analysis of what had been done and how it had been done was done at that level. What I can say on my part is that I wasn't invited to participate in the analysis of how this action had been executed, and therefore, I'm unable to give you anything more than I already have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the next half, the latter half, of 1999, could you describe for us briefly, however, the activities of the SAJ units in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring Mr. Trajkovic to the latter part of 1998. Was there in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the transcript, line 13, there should be State Security Service, whereas the transcript says "date security service."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a major anti-terrorist offensive that commenced sometime in the latter half of 1998, and did the SAJ participate in it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the second half of 1998 there had been a joint staff set up composed of the command of the Pristina Corps and command of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. So the Serbian security forces were ordered to clear up the area of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija from terrorist activities and to take terrorists to court so that the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija could be placed under the control of the Serbian security forces. Our units participated in those actions in accordance with the plans that had been approved at the Joint Command level, and all the way up until the end of September 1998 we took part in the actions that had been planned in this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that a joint staff was set up and later on you said a Joint Command. Is -- was this body that coordinated the VJ and the MUP referred to as the joint staff or the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you tell us about when this body was formed.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in late June/early July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were you a member of this command, the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was a member of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, and only the top leadership of our command together with the command of the Pristina Corps comprised the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could you, as best as you can - I know you probably will not be able to include everybody - but could you name all the persons you know who were members of the Joint Command at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen a document concerning the Joint Command, but I would say based on the posts of people who were there at the time it was the commander of the Pristina Corps at the time, Mr. Nebojsa Pavkovic; his deputy and Chief of Staff, Mr. Lazarevic; I think that Mr. Djakovic also belonged there as an operations officer of the Pristina Corps; and that on behalf of the MUP Mr. Sreten Lukic was a member; and most likely his deputy, David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if any members of the political leadership participated in the deliberations of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1998 there was a number of politicians who were present in the territory of Kosovo. They wanted to add to the importance and significance of all the actions that were carried out by the security forces, the army, and the police. Now, as to whether they participated in the decision-making process, I don't know, but there was a number of politicians in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At that time and during these anti-terrorist operations, did members of the leadership of the MUP come to Kosovo and participate in the work of the MUP in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: During the period of time that we're discussing now in the territory of Kosovo, there were mostly Generals Djordjevic and Stevanovic present in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija on behalf of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know what was the nature of their participation in the work of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: What I know and what I saw in the field was that both Mr. Stevanovic and Mr. Djordjevic were frequently present in the territory of Kosovo and that they even appeared on the ground where certain units carried out operations. As for Mr. Djordjevic, I can say that he frequently was with our units when we were in the field. And as to their participation in the decisions that were adopted at the level of the Joint Command, I don't know about that; however, their presence during that period of time was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if they remained in Kosovo all the time or if they would return to Belgrade from time to time for meetings or other affairs of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer I didn't mean to say that they were present in Kosovo throughout, that they never went back. But what I meant to say was that they were more often present than in the period of time prior to that. And depending on what duties they had, they would go back to Belgrade for one, two, three days and then they would come back. And either both of them would be present in Kosovo or at least one of them would be present. Their presence was more pronounced at the time, most likely because there was a lot of activity on behalf of the MUP in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and that's why their presence was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djordjevic at any time indicate to you what his attitude was towards his presence in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On one hand, I understood that his presence as well as the presence of the politicians in Kosovo at the time was meant to express the importance or underline the importance and significance of all the actions and operations that we had there at the time. I remember that once I jokingly asked him, "Boss, why are you so often in Kosovo these days?" And he replied, also jokingly, "I'm safer here than in Belgrade." We didn't comment on what he said, but I think that in the discussions and interviews I've had so far I've mentioned this, what he said, that he was safer here than in Belgrade. But we didn't specifically comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like briefly to show you a document. This is a document that's in evidence, it's P886. These are the minutes of the meeting of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to page 57 in the English and 59 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think I'm mistaken, but when Mr. Stamp posed a question, the witness said that he did not attend the meetings of the body that he refers to as the Joint Command. And now what is being put to him are the minutes from some meeting of the Joint Command. I think that we should first establish whether he is aware of the existence of this document rather than try to present this document immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp will conduct his examination as he sees fit, but if he goes beyond the point where the evidence would support him, we will stop him. Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we scroll down in the Serbian version. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the notes for the 23rd of August, 1998, and you see in the middle of the page there there's a record of what General Djordjevic contributed to that meeting and his conclusion at the end in respect to the Belgrade and Prizren companies of the SAJ proceeding along the Dulje-Rance direction. I just wanted to indicate to the Court whether there was, in fact, this operation that General Djordjevic is referring to, if your units acted as indicated there.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the last line it says: "Prizren company, Belgrade company, and the SAJ to proceed along the Dulje-Rance axis." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall your units engaging in that action at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on these notes, I'm unable to see the context. I don't know what this whole action was about. It says here -- it says that this is a conclusion and that the Prizren company and the Belgrade company and the SAJ were to proceed along the Dulje-Rance direction. At that period of time, yes, we were present in this area and in other areas. We covered on foot the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and most likely we were present in this area along this axis as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But specifically can you recall if your unit was engaged to proceed along the Dulje-Rance axis?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all in respect to this document. Can you tell us briefly, Mr. Trajkovic, what was the respective roles of the different units of the MUP, for example, the PJP and the SAJ, as well as the VJ in anti-terrorist actions or combat? In the normal situation how were they organised in the offensives against KLA positions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The first half of 1998 was characterised by police operations with weapons and equipment that we had, and then from the moment when the Joint Command was formed and the planning of operations for future periods began, the operations were mainly carried out jointly. On various axes various units were active. The Special Anti-Terrorist Units mostly were engaged where the terrorist groups had their strongholds, and when our forces advanced, if there was combat, then we would also be engaged when the regular MUP forces could not resolve such tasks, that was when the members of the SAJ were introduced to break through such parts of the territory and the members of the SAJ [as interpreted] were mainly in charge of holding the positions on the flanks. As for the Yugoslav Army, we had their support at the time in the sense that they would fire in order to unblock --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. The record here - and I don't think that is what you said - said that members of the SAJ were mainly in charge of holding positions on the flanks. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said that the focus of the activities of the SAJ were where the terrorists had their strongholds and that the flanks were held by members of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's the PJP?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were just about to go on to tell us about the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The role of the Yugoslav Army in this period was that of fire support, providing fire support, and we often used their combat armoured vehicles because they had inexperienced young soldiers in this territory, and usually we used those joint units with our members in order to break through until the moment of combat with terrorists. And it was possible for them to break through because they used the armoured vehicles of the Yugoslav Army, and this was more or less how all the actions in the field were carried out in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about 1999, was that the same way you normally conducted the operations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: 1999 is more specific in terms of the activities of our forces, because on the 24th of March the NATO aggression, the air-strikes, were launched and targets that were of vital importance for our armed forces were being hit so that the units of the Yugoslav Army, as they were highly visible targets, used to camouflage themselves and to get closer to the sectors where the actions were carried out. And only occasionally they could be engaged by firing from their weapons so that they would not be spotted by the NATO radars even though the command remained at the same level, that is to say, there was a Joint Command and the state of war was declared. By contrast with 1998, the focus of our activities was in addition to fighting terrorist groups, which had additional zest to participate in even greater numbers in the activities they had started, the focus of the activities of the forces of the army and the members of our service was to defend the state territory and to prepare for this defence, defend the territory from a possible land invasion of NATO forces against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said the VJ would provide fire support and they could be engaged by firing from their weapons, what precisely do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly mortars, mortar support, and if the situation was even more difficult then sometimes fire from tanks was used as well in order to break through barricades or strongholds that were harder to break through. But because of the factor that this could make them very visible, this was very rarely used during 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier you had indicated that you acted in accordance with plans approved at the Joint Command level. Did you receive your orders to engage in combat actions orally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly written orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who or which body would you or your command or your unit commanders get these orders from?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Just like in 1998, during 1999 we got excerpts from these orders which related to the engagement and participation. Specifically if it were -- if these were my units, then this would relate to the participation of my unit in a specific action and our coordinated action with the units that were superior to the PJP units and the units of the Yugoslav Army. And probably the same excerpts from these orders that were adopted at the Joint Command were also received by the members of the Yugoslav Army for such specific tasks when that was the situation. And we received these even though the location of our staffs used to change very often, we always knew where they were located. We would drop by for a short visit. We would receive the excerpts from these orders. And when we were in the situation to drop by briefly after we had carried out the actions, we would go there and brief them, we would tell them how the action had been carried out, and then we would go to our final destination, that is to say, where our own units were quartered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you said you would drop by to the location where your staffs were to visit. When you say "staff," which entity are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija. Our staff continued to operate just like in 1998, that is where Mr. Lukic and possibly a man he had appointed, it could be on one day Mr. David Gajic or one of his other associates, they would go to the meetings of the Joint Command, and I did not know this because in 1999 I did not attend any of these official meetings, so that I could tell where each staff was located, but for our MUP staff we always knew where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Joint Command orders that were excerpted, did you have any opportunity to see any of these Joint Command orders during 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: For every action I received the excerpts from the orders, as I said, and the excerpts usually said -- sometimes I didn't pay much attention to that, but sometimes the heading said "MUP staff." Sometimes it was the "Joint Command staff." But mostly the orders that we received said, I think, the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of documents, Mr. Trajkovic, and ask you a couple of questions about them. Firstly, could we look at D104, please, that's the exhibit number. It's 65 ter 01966. This is a Joint Command order to quote it: "To rout and destroy the STS in the Malo Kosovo area ..." Did you have an opportunity recently to have a look at this document? And can you recall if the action to which this order refers to actually took place?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the orders, and it's probable that this happened. But as far as I can see, it's an order that relates to units of the Yugoslav Army. It's an excerpt from the order that was adopted at the Joint Command. It's probable that the second half or the other part of such an order was either headed the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija or it had the same heading but a different text. Because here in the first line the tasks of the Yugoslav Army units are mentioned, and we received such orders, but in the first line the tasks of our units were emphasised and then the coordinated action with the units of the Yugoslav Army would be mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Perhaps if I give to you, with the leave of the Court, a hard copy of the document, you could just look through it and tell us whether or not your unit participated or any of your units participated in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we go to the English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trajkovic, in your copy that's -- I don't know the page in Serbian, but that's on the section 5: "Tasks for the units."

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the task for the 22nd -- the 22nd of March, and I arrived on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija on the 23rd of March in the afternoon. But I think a part of our unit from Pristina, that's the SAJ Pristina, participated in this action, and I think that two of our members were killed on that occasion. However, I was not present in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at the time, but I remember this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to be sure that I understand your evidence, Mr. Trajkovic, the -- on many occasions, on most occasions, the Joint Command orders would be excerpted and your unit would receive an excerpt that referred specifically to the task of your unit. Is that a correct --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And many times the document you received was an excerpt done by the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of a joint plan which was adopted at the level of the Joint Command, the Pristina Corps command prepared excerpts from the joint decision to carry out certain tasks for the Yugoslav Army units. And mostly the command of the MUP staff for the Kosovo and Metohija did it for the police units where my units also belonged. They prepared excerpts from these, firstly emphasising the tasks of the units of the Ministry of the Interior, and then the next tasks that were emphasized were those that were to be carried out jointly with the units of the Yugoslav Army. And more or less that was how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have now a look at 65 ter 1968, and this is Exhibit P971. And perhaps with the leave of the Court I could hand to the witness a hard copy and retrieve the one that he has. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the action or the operation referred to in this order? Do you know if this operation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the said day my units were on a completely different axis, and therefore I do not know if this operation was conducted or not. But if this is original material then it's probable that the action was carried out. But as I say, on the said day my unit was in a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to 65 ter 01878, and again I would like to hand the witness a hard copy to expedite the proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: An order for an operation of the 15th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Just like with the previous document, as soon as I saw the heading of this order I could tell that my units were not present in this territory, that is the territory from Pec towards the Republic of Montenegro. None of my units were in this area at the time, but again, as I say, the document is of the kind that I used to see. But whether the operation was conducted or not and in what way, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness having identified the document as similar to those which emanate from the Joint Command that he used to see, and I think on the face of the document and at the end of the document one can see that it has the stamps and other numbering, subject numbering, similar to other Joint Command orders that have been received in evidence, on that basis I would respectfully tender it and ask that this one be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, considering the criteria that we adopted, I have no objections whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01328.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And lastly in this vein could we look at document 19 -- sorry, it's -- it's 65 ter 01976, and it's Exhibit P767. And again I would with the leave of the Court give the witness a hard copy and recover the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a Joint Command order of the 15th of April, 1999 for operation in the area of Jezerce. Do you know whether or not this order or this operation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Please excuse me. My units did participate in a similar action, but as this is only an excerpt intended for the army units, the units or forces of the MUP are not more specifically mentioned, and I cannot really conclude if this is the action I have in mind or not. But roughly at this time our units did have a task to carry out in this sector. So I cannot say with certainty if this is the task that my units had the special police units and the SAJ in coordinated action with the Yugoslav Army units. But around this time, the 15th of April, it's possible that it relates to this action. But if we had the excerpts from the order relating to the MUP units, then one could see with more detail which were the units that participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm wondering if this is a convenient time? Especially since my friend I think has a submission to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the convenient time for the break, but I wanted to speak to Mr. Stamp during the break so as not to trouble the Chamber with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. We will have our first break now. This is a break for half an hour. A court officer will assist you during the break, and we'll resume at a quarter past 4.00, continue questioning after that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we broke off, Mr. Trajkovic, we were looking at a document which I still think is on the screen in front of you, and that is document P767. If we could look at page 4 of the English and page 2 of the Serbian version very briefly. Just the top at "Readiness." The document is dated the 14th of April, 1999. But you see here that it -- it says: "Readiness. "For routing and destroying the STS in the area of Jezerce at 0600 hours on the 23rd of April, 1999." Have you seen that section?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And does that help you to recall in any way whether or not your units or any of your units were involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once again I repeat that my units were present in this territory, but whether this document pertains to exactly that order is something I cannot claim with certainty. As I have told you, it would have been of great help if we had the excerpt pertaining to the MUP forces because that document would list each unit that participated in that action. Here I cannot see any indication of what MUP units were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps we could move on from that. During that period 1998 -- sorry, in 1999, that's March, April, May, could the SAJ be engaged by the Joint Command without the overall sanction or authorisation of the leadership of the MUP, including the minister and the head of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the leadership of the MUP cede authority to engage or to sanction the engagement of the forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once an immediate threat of war was declared and also when the state of war was introduced, it was taken for granted that all units that had been sent by the minister of the interior - I'm now referring to the MUP units - are to be placed under the command of the Joint Command of the army and MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. This was an understatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, an understatement or an understanding that you had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I took the situation, that's what I took it to mean, and that's how it was. And it applied to all the units that were sent there. We have to distinguish between the peacetime and between the time when there was an immediate threat of war declared as well as the state of war. The order of the minister of the interior indicated that all of the units that had been sent there and that were there pursuant to that order, that were sent there to carry out the tasks of the ministry, once they were there in Kosovo during that period of time they were duty-bound to carry out the orders and accept tasks issued to them by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on to look briefly at the MUP staff. Do you know when the MUP staff was set up and what was its role or function?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija dates back to 1981 with certain changes. At that time it was the staff of the then-Federal Secretariat of the Interior. And up until 1991 members representing all republics and provinces of the old Yugoslavia were sent there due to the disturbances in the law and order system. And then starting in 1993, members of the Ministry of the Interior from Serbia were sent there, and they were under the command of the staff, and the composition of the staff changed as did the units that were sent to Kosovo. They dealt with the problems existing at that period of time. And then in 1998 and 1999 - and I think that you're trying to focus on that period of time - in 1998 -- or maybe even in 1997 the staff for Kosovo and Metohija was set up. And all the way up until the end of 1999 or until the withdrawal of our forces from Kosovo and Metohija, that staff existed as the staff of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia for the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And this staff was given special prominence in the second half of 1998 and in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter number 01505 and that's P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a decision to establish the ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism of the 16th of June, 1998. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At approximately the time when it was issued, did you receive a copy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we can see here - perhaps scroll down a little bit on the Serbian version - that you are -- your name is there as a member of the staff, the assistant head for the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivko Trajkovic. Were you a member of the staff? You were saying that you attended its meetings and participated in its deliberations.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were three of us assistants that were designated as assistants for special operations, for staff units, and assistants for special police units; and pursuant to our posts, we were ex officio members of the staff in view of the tasks that we were to carry even though we seldom took part of the work of the staff and in planning. Because, as I have stated in my previous answers, most actions during this period of time were planned at the level of the Joint Command together with the command of the Pristina Corps, whereas we in our meetings received excerpts concerning the actions that we were to carry out and also gave briefing concerning our activities immediately after the completed actions. At that time our headquarters were in the then-building of the Pristina secretariat or the Ministry of the Interior and there were premises where we could meet and talk about the actions that had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the unnecessary typing please stop from the Prosecutor's desk. There is a lot of noise and the interpreters are having problems hearing the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on briefly to look at 01989, this is P764.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the minutes of a meeting of the MUP staff on the 4th of April, 1999. Can you recall attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think if we move on to -- I think it's page 7 of the English -- sorry, page 3 of the English, which is also page 3 of the B/C/S copy indicates that you participated in this meeting in your capacity as head of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall about how many such meetings you participated in during the conflict -- during the NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the conflict and during the NATO intervention, there was perhaps another one or none at all of such meetings. I know that I attended one. Now, as to whether we attended another meeting of this kind or not, I cannot remember. I cannot remember attending a meeting with this expanded list of attendees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we -- if we could take down that document and put up 01990, that's P85. Can you recall seeing Mr. Djordjevic in Kosovo, or do you recall his attendance in Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Unlike 1998, Mr. Djordjevic carried out most of his activities in the territory of Serbia, and he came to Kosovo once or twice -- at least I met him on those occasions, and I didn't hear about him coming there more often than twice perhaps to my knowledge. And I think that one of those occasions was before the NATO intervention and the other time during it. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this -- these are the minutes of a meeting of the 17th of February, 1999, and you see he's in attendance there, and it's also indicated that the head of the SAJ's also in attendance. Do you recall attending that meeting at the staff of the 17th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that because the minister also attended, the late Vlajko Stojiljkovic, and both chiefs of departments. So I remember this meeting, that was on the 17th of February, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mr. Lukic and Mr. -- and the minister, Mr. Stojiljkovic, made presentations at this meeting in respect to the forthcoming offensive?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene because Mr. Stamp asks about what happened at the meeting and then he goes on to say "in respect to the forthcoming offensive." I would ask that the questions be simplified so that the witness doesn't talk about -- doesn't have to talk about what happened at the meeting and in the forthcoming offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I think the witness understood the question. The question I just asked was whether at the meeting the forthcoming offensive were discussed, not a question about the forthcoming offensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us earlier, Mr. Trajkovic - and I'm moving on to something else now - that you were assigned to operations in Kosovo on the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- we don't have an answer to your question on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you want one or have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The answer was "yes." I heard yes, but I'm unsure if it's on the record, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, there was no ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecutor put this question to me, I understood it to mean the NATO offensive against our country that was becoming more and more evident. That's how I understood it to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And -- and at that meeting Mr. Lukic and Mr. Stojiljkovic addressed those present as to what the duties and tasks of the MUP units would be at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in case there was a NATO aggression. I think that you can find that formulation somewhere in the minutes. What I remember is that this meeting was called in order to highlight the tasks that would be given to the MUP units should there be a NATO aggression. Because the tasks that were carried out during that period of time probably would not have been carried out had there not been a NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And moving on, you personally, not the unit now, you were assigned to take part directly in operations in Kosovo on the 22nd of March, 1999? I think that's what you told us earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. As immediately before that, that is to say upon the completion of operations in late September 1998, I returned to my post in Belgrade and then I was sent back to the territory of Kosovo around -- I think it said on the 22nd, but I arrived there on the 23rd in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 24th and the 25th of March were you and any of your units engaged in any action or activity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Our task was to carry out coordinated action with the units of the Yugoslav Army and special police units to engage from the direction of Kursumlija, which is located on the territory of Serbia, in order to suppress the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Palane, Gornja and Donja Repa, then also the village of Krpimej, Bradas, and all the way to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could focus on Podujevo for a few minutes, Mr. Trajkovic. You're aware that at about that time a group of men known as the Skorpions were incorporated into the SAJ in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this formulation of the question because it contains a statement and also the name of a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You need to introduce this subject matter with the knowledge of the witness, not with your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. I really thought that that aspect was not in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall if any of your units was augmented by any group of reservists at approximately that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this group of reservists known by any particular name?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This group of reservists got its name later on, that is to say it was identified with the name of a combat group which fought in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and this name was identified with this group of reservists that was attached to our unit because the commander of this group, and that is to say the officer of this group who was to join our unit, was the commander of the Skorpions unit that was active in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and as I learned later, also in the territory of I think Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when did it -- did this group begin to be referred to as the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The reference to them as Skorpions began I believe in around 1994 or 1995 or maybe even 1993. I'm not sure. Because it was approximately formed as a group that was to secure the oilfields in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or, more specifically, in the sector of Mirkovci where the oilfield was and also in order to secure the border with the Belgrade-Zagreb highway near Adasevci. That was the end of their sector. And later on this group became a unit, but when exactly the symbols and emblems of the Skorpions appeared I cannot say with any certainty, but I think it was the time-period that I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time they were incorporated into the SAJ in 1999, who contacted you with a view to effecting that purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As our units were weakened because they took part in operations in 1999 and considering the fact that the whole SAJ unit from Novi Sad was re-deployed by a decision of the minister [Realtime translation read in error "ministry"], it was attached to the special operations unit of the State Security Service, and considering the requests from both the minister and the leadership of the MUP that the SAJ units should contribute to the combat against the Siptar terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999 and especially in defending the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, I pointed out this problem, that we had a lack of men, that the number of men was smaller than the numbers that we had in 1998. And I talked to my immediate superior, and that was Mr. Djordjevic, and it was only natural that he should be the first that I talked to. And as at the time of our engagement was getting close, we talked more and more often about replenishing our units so that we could carry out the serious tasks that were ahead of us. In this period beginning with the 24th and the beginning of the NATO intervention in the territory of Kosovo, I contacted Mr. Djordjevic, and he told me that one combat group was ready to join us. At the time, as we were involved in carrying out one specific task, I could not give any kind of approval, and I said that we should wait with this until the action that had been launched was completed and until we were able to receive this unit in an adequate manner because we needed some means of transportation for them, and we did not have anything attached to us for the transportation of these people because we could not drive them through the territory of Kosovo in buses. And they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 34, line 4, it should be stated that the minister took this decision and not the ministry. I was afraid that the transcript would just continue, so it was the decision of the minister. Line 35 -- page 35, line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- with the witness, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, whose decision was it to re-deploy the Novi Sad unit to the special operations unit of the state security?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It could have been done only at the order of the minister. I know that in connection with this I contacted and talked to my immediate superior, Mr. Djordjevic, and when I asked him why this was being done he told me, "What can I tell you when nobody asked me anything about this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to the incorporation of the unit into the SAJ. On the 24th you said -- and the 25th you were engaged in operations in the field in Kosovo. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the engagement of these men, who contacted who?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to note one thing that might be important for the way this combat group was engaged. The Special Anti-Terrorist Units do not have reserve forces according to their systemisation, but as there was a need to replenish the SAJ unit, to replenish them with men for the forthcoming tasks, we could only do that through the police administration which had within its composition a squad for mobilisation, that is to say a squad of reserve forces. Before I went to Kosovo and Metohija to carry out specific tasks, I talked several times with Mr. Djordjevic about the best way and about the possible way in which our units could be replenished with a combat group. And at the time we did not have any specific resolution for this, but I asked him to find some possibility for some combat group to be attached to our forces. So sometime around the 25th or so I received information from him that one combat group was ready, that it was now part of the reserve forces of the MUP, and that it would be in the sector bordering Kosovo and Metohija. And later on I learned that this group was quartered at the Prolom spa, that was a place immediately next to the border with Kosovo. I noted at the time that in our conversation I said that we should wait before this unit was introduced, and we should see when the preconditions would be met for it to be introduced so that we could do all that in the safest possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say that you should wait to see when the preconditions would be met? What preconditions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that as our units were quite mobile we kept moving from one area to another. So in order to be able to receive them, we would have to see together with the staff if we would have some field vehicles ready to bring these people to the place where they would be quartered. So first of all I had this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about their training and their suitability for action on behalf of the police, was it a precondition in your mind?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but considering the situation that we were in we certainly wouldn't have given these men operational tasks. We simply needed a number of men who would physically secure the places where our units were quartered and accommodated and also in the field so as to have the shifts and change the people who were tired and exhausted in the field because we would be in the field for three or four days. And for these tasks no special training was necessary, and I received the information that this was a team and a combat group that had already carried out the tasks of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In conversation with Mr. Djordjevic I learned that these were experienced or partly experienced combatants who had already been at the fronts in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, by what means did you speak with Mr. Djordjevic at the time? Through what medium of communication?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that once we talked by cell phone and on the 27th of March I called Mr. Djordjevic on the telephone from the police department in Podujevo before we had our accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you normally use mobile phones during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not usual, but for passing on very important and short information we had to contact one another because we didn't have any other means of communication when we were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the PJP commanders, did they have that facility as well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time all officers in the MUP, so beginning in 1993 or 1994 they all had cell phones available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And back to where we were in respect to -- before I go on, these cell phones that they had available, they were operational during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that on the 24th and 25th until around the 27th one could still use them. I'm not sure about the later period. I cannot be certain, but I think that by the 26th or the 27th the phones could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to the engagement of the unit. You said that you told Mr. Djordjevic when he contacted you about this unit to wait because you wanted to do your checks on certain preconditions. What happened after that? Were you able to do what you intended to do?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, because when I got back after our conversation, that is to say after I called the staff and Mr. Djordjevic, we had an accident. The vehicle that I was in came across an anti-tank mine and hit it, and on this occasion the driver who had been driving me for a number of years was killed, and two other persons from my escort, that was an analyst and another person, were wounded seriously and so was I. And so after this incident, together with the driver and the analyst, I was transported to the Pristina hospital. And the person who was a member of the escort who was with us, he remained in Podujevo. He didn't want to go to the hospital because he felt that he was fit enough to continue working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened in respect to these men that Mr. Djordjevic spoke to you about or that you discussed with Mr. Djordjevic while you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned later that Mr. Simovic -- when Mr. Djordjevic was informed about this incident agreed with Mr. Simovic that this unit be introduced and that later on -- as it was expected that we would stay in Podujevo for several days, that they would see with the staff how they would secure the means of transportation for these people. And together with his driver he went to Prolom Banja, which is very close to Podujevo, and he escorted these men to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. -- I think there might just be an error here. When Mr. Djordjevic was informed about the incident agreed with Mr. Simovic -- it seems here from the record that you are saying Mr. Simovic agreed with Mr. Simovic. Can you just explain what arrangements were made in respect to these men while you were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I hope I said with Mr. Djordjevic, with General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So do I take it that you mean when Mr. Djordjevic was informed of the -- of the fact that you were injured, Mr. Simovic agreed with him on the introduction of these men?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could remind us or maybe if I could just ask you if that's correct. Mr. Simovic was the commander of the Belgrade unit of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in hospital did you receive information about what happened in respect to these men on the 28th of March, 1999, at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we are talking about the 27th of March because they were introduced immediately after I was taken to the hospital, unless I'm mistaken, but I think that this all took place on the same day and that was the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But there was just around that time an incident in Podujevo involving these men. Did you learn about that incident while you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about it on the next day, on the 28th. I can't remember who was the officer who came to visit me, but he informed me about what had happened immediately after the arrival of this combat group to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did you learn had happened? If you could tell us very briefly in just a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: During their arrival to the territory of Podujevo, their commander, Slobodan Medic, together with the commanders of the Pristina and Belgrade SAJs, Mr. Simovic and Mr. Stanojevic [as interpreted], went to our command which was in Podujevo, our temporary command in Podujevo. And the men were told that they should find accommodation in a street that they were assigned to. While the men were being accommodated in these streets, one or two, I'm not sure how many streets were assigned for their accommodation, they came across civilians, mostly women, children, and the elderly, and the incident happened at that time. The information I had was that they were provoked in one way or another, these perpetrators, that several members of the police provoked them in the sense of, "What are you waiting for? Our commander has been injured. Why don't you do away with these people in front of you?" This is the information that I got from several members of this unit later when I went to disarm this unit and send it back to where it had come from. On that occasion many people were killed, all of them civilians, women and children, I don't know the exact number. When word spread about this shoot-out the commanding officers ran out to see what was going on and immediately an ambulance team was called and the doctor that we had attached to our unit. And then they offered the first aid, as much of it as was possible, and care was provided to the women and children. Some of them were sent to the Pristina hospital, but unfortunately there was no way to save a number of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- or should I put it this way: Do you know what was done in respect of these men, that is, the unit that had been incorporated immediately after some members shot these civilians in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This unit did not remain more than 30 minutes in the Podujevo area, and the commanders that remained on site, Mr. Simovic and Stanojevic [as interpreted], informed the staff in Pristina and Mr. Djordjevic that this unit is to be sent back immediately to Prolom Banja and that later on they would see what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they sent back?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That unit could not remain there, to send them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they sent back to Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see here on the record that you said that the commanders, Mr. Simovic and Mr. Stanojevic, who remained on site did certain things. Is it Stanojevic, or who were the commanders who were there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Stalevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see earlier that you said that later you went to disarm the unit and send it back to where it had come from. Can you just elaborate upon that. Where did you go to disarm the unit and when?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once I was discharged from the hospital in Pristina, I was sent to Belgrade to continue my treatment at home. At that time I was in Belgrade. I got in touch with Mr. Djordjevic, and we were considering what to do, and he then asked me whether I could go in order to bring that unit back to Belgrade. Since the police department in charge of mobilisation had issued them with weapons they were to be disarmed and then sent home. I responded to him by saying that it would be good if Mr. Milanovic went with me because he knew personally Mr. Medic. And Mr. Djordjevic agreed with me. I mentioned at the time that we would carry out that assignment without any problem. I spoke to Mr. Milanovic and I asked him whether he would be willing to come with me to carry out this assignment. He agreed without any objection, and I don't know how many days after this event, after this incident, we went first to the secretariat in Pristina, where we informed the then-chief of the secretariat -- rather, the police department in Prokuplje about what was our intention, what we were going to do; namely, that the unit which was in their territory would be sent back to Belgrade. Then we went to Prolom Banja. The unit was lined up. I told them that the unit was going back to Belgrade, that they would return the weapons in the location where they had been issued with weapons, and that it was yet to be decided what was going to be done with them, and that we would timely inform them via their commander. And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This Mr. Milanovic that you referred to, could you tell us his full name and whether or not he was known by any nicknames so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milan Milanovic, nicknamed Mrgud.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many of these men in total did you discover had been incorporated into your units?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In that first deployment, according to the lists that were prepared for the payment of compensation, that there were 128 members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what type of weapons were they issued with?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Classic -- typical infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Like what?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, AKM-47 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were there at around that time formal investigations in the murder of these women and children at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I wasn't out on the ground, but I was informed that immediately after the incident an on-site investigation was carried out and that this came under the responsibility of the investigations department from Prokuplje. They were to investigate this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to the case at that time was -- in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Given that the war was still on, I don't know whether they stood trial immediately. I don't know whether the investigating judge instituted any proceedings, but I know that initially the proceedings were instituted against two or three members and that it wasn't until 2002 or 2003 when they gathered all of the information about the number of people who had taken part in that crime. Now it is well-known that all of us -- all of those who had participated in that crime were brought to justice and that they were sentenced to appropriate prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that all of the men who participated in that crime were sentenced?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I learned that in that first trial not everybody was indicted, and then later on in 2002 and 2003 they acknowledged the dimensions of this case. And all of the -- those who participated in this event stood trial and were sentenced to long prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the case in 1999 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember with certainty, but I think that in the initial judgement, whether it was a judgement or perhaps it was just a decision by the investigating judge -- I don't know that -- there was a debate about it. They said that the investigating judge did not act appropriately so the case was dismissed, and then there was another proceedings instituted. So initially there were just two or three people indicted, and later on all of those who participated were included in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
