utterances.text: I think -- or before I get to that, when you went and spoke to the Skorpions to disarm them, did you -- were they given leave of absence before that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time when you went to meet with the Skorpions and to disarm them, did you or anybody indicate to them that they would be allowed a leave of absence from their duties?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that it would be allowed, but as a result of this incident which took place an order was issued that they were to return back to the initial location from which they had come and that they were to surrender the weapons that they had been issued with at the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to interrupt Mr. Stamp until the entire answer were given, but once again the question was phrased as disarmament of the Skorpions. And up until now the witness has never used that term, whereas Mr. Stamp insists on using that term in his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answers of the witness have accepted that term and explained how it came to be used, as I understand. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier on you refer -- you referred to the first engagement of the Skorpions, indicating that there was perhaps a next engagement. Were they re-engaged at any time to any unit under your command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the name, the Skorpions, in some of my earlier statements and interviews with The Hague investigators I mentioned how the Prosecution accepted this name, the Skorpions; and I think that previously I mentioned that since their commander was the commander of a unit which had been in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem but which did not have any significant contacts with that unit except that the commander of this combat group was Slobodan Medic and that within that unit as far as I know and as we learned later, 15 or 16 members of that unit were investigated. This is how this name came to be accepted. Even in our lists for the payment of per diems and other expenses, due to Mr. Slobodan Medic that group came to be known as the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we could get back on track here. Was there re-engagement of the Skorpions to the SAJ in Kosovo during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 5, line 5 it says: "... members of that unit were investigated," which is not true. The witness said something quite different, that it was established that only 15 members of that earlier unit were now members of this new unit and not that they were under investigation. I think that I heard it well in, Serbian, and they were not under investigation. That's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you sort that out, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, you heard what Mr. Djurdjic just said. Did you -- what did you mean when you referred to the 15 or 16 members of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that 15 or 16 members of the unit belonged to the unit which in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was known under the name the Skorpions. And those people participated in this other event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, that's a new element. What other event are you speaking of now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that 15 or 16 members of this combat group which had been deployed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija earlier on were members of the Skorpions unit. And when I -- I said this when I explained how this name, the Skorpions, came about. And I said that due to the commander, Slobodan Medic, this group came to be known as the Skorpions, but that it was not the same unit that had previously been in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there another event that you are aware of that this unit participated in?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, sometime in 2000 -- I'm not sure whether it was 2006 or 2007, we saw what was broadcast by the media about how this group had had an incident in the territory of Bosnia, this unit known as the Skorpions. I think it was in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Thank you. Back to Kosovo in 1999 during the conflict there. Was the unit re-engaged; and if so, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: This crime received quite a lot of publicity in Serbia, and I know that Slobodan Milosevic asked for reports about what had happened there. I know that the commanders, Mr. Simovic and Stalevic, wrote reports about that. They had to explain what had happened and how in the territory of Podujevo. Later on -- and when I came to Belgrade to continue my treatment at home, when I spent a number of days in Belgrade I had an opportunity to meet with Mr. Djordjevic and with Mr. Milanovic, and that we discussed this tragic event and that as far as we were concerned that case could be considered as an excessive crime. And that the entire unit did not have to suffer consequences for what happened because, after all, these people went as reservists to defend the territory of Kosovo and that we would see what could be done about that. I came back to the territory of Kosovo several days later and our units had been issued tasks and assignments in a rural area, that is to say we had a huge territory to cover and not enough people for that. And we pointed out this fact in our previous reports, that under those circumstances we had to carry out our assignments. And that the part of the unit which did not take part in this unfortunate event should be cleared of any guilt, and that had I been in the territory of Podujevo this incident would not have happened most likely. And that for as long as I remained there, there would be no further incidents. And we came to the conclusion that we needed men and we could not count on receiving any reinforcement. And at that time the possibility of land invasion by NATO was becoming more and more certain so that somewhat later in Belgrade it was decided that -- or rather, some men did not want to join, and those who had taken part in this unfortunate event were left out. And that according to the list, 108 of them joined our units in Kosovo Polje, which is where our headquarters was located at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that it was decided in Belgrade. Just tell us precisely who decided to do what?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The three of us talked how should there be a need, this unit should be deployed again. But naturally, given that the staff in Pristina was the only body with authority to issue such approval, a report was sent to the staff in Pristina explaining the newly emerged situation, namely, that our unit needed reinforcement, needed additional men, and that we would set up a new unit that would exclude those who had participated in the incident. And I think that there was some people who were ill and some people who did not wish to be included, engaged as part of reserve forces. So in the first list we had 128 members of that unit, and then in the new list there were 108 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Who in the police chain of command made the decision to re-engage them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the decision made in Belgrade and the agreement with the staff in Pristina about the engagement of reserve forces, it is always the minister who makes the decision. But he can always delegate this decision to an officer of a lower rank to implement it. I don't know if there was a written order to engage this reserve unit or not, but then the decision to engage reserve forces always has to be taken by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you met with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that something was left out here when he says that the minister could delegate this to somebody else, that the decision could be realised or carried out. I think that this was left out from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to ask anything more about that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that can be clarified by Mr. Djurdjic if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, are you still on the same subject, or are you moving to another?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am on the same subject, but I will be on it for about five to ten minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that case we better have the second break now, and we'll resume at a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, I think you mentioned earlier that you had been interviewed by the OTP and you answered certain questions.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you answer these questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I mostly did but I have to note that I was in a specific situation, especially as concerns my interview with ICTY investigators. It was the moment when I was a suspect in relation to the events that we are discussing now, and I might have answered some questions with minor changes of details not with intention to not tell the truth. But I might have believed at that time that it suited me better to formulate my answers the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very good. Did you say anything which was not true to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have not been in the situation to study in detail all my statements and all my answers, but I can freely say that more than 90 per cent of what I said was really so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is: To your knowledge, do you recall saying anything which was not true?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot know with certainty whether it would not be correct if I said that I was certain because had I had the chance to study all the interviews and all the statements in detail then I could say with more certainty when replying to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are in the direct examination and the witness is answering about the facts that the representative of the Prosecution is asking him about. I don't see how we can talk about this when there was no reason and no cause to discuss this. And another thing, as far as I can see, there are questions about a statement which the witness gave as a suspect. But since February or January this year when you made the decision that he would be on the list of witnesses, if he gave any statements he could give them as a statement [as interpreted] and he shouldn't be asked now about the interviews, not the statement, but the interview that he had with the investigations from the Prosecution. I think that this is not appropriate for the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The subject matter is an obvious one. The question asked is clear and straightforward and is not leading in form, and the answer could have been most material. So for the moment, Mr. Djurdjic, the Chamber does not accept the point of your objection. In any event, it appears not to have affected the course of the proceedings. Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you met with Mr. Milanovic and Mr. Djordjevic on more than one occasion in Belgrade to discuss the return or the possible re-engagement of the unit. Who decided that they should be re-engaged in Serbia -- in Kosovo with your SAJ units?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noted in one of my previous answers that the engagement of the reserve police forces is approved by the minister of the interior. Now, whether he makes the decision directly or whether he allows some of his subordinates the right to do that, it depends on the situation. As our situation at the time was very specific -- and, for example, I didn't know whether Mr. Djordjevic and Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic could see each other at the time or not -- I just know that we agreed this at one of our meetings and that I proposed at the time that if it was approved again that this combat group should join my units, that I could guarantee everything about their engagement and that there would be no unfortunate incidents or, God forbid, a crime. Whoever issued this order, I'm not sure about that. I only received information from Mr. Djordjevic that this unit would be engaged again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About when was this that you received this information and about when were they re-engaged?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was approximately in mid-April 1999 or, I would say, in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we bring up P86. Could we quickly look on the last page. This is a memorandum to the assistant minister, the chief of the public service department -- public security department, Mr. Djordjevic. Could we just go to the last page in both the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's your signature there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps if we return to the first page briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is just for clarification. It's not dated. Can you tell us about that, if you know why?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see in the upper part of the first page -- I cannot see the heading where it just says "Belgrade." It is usual that above that in the upper left-hand corner there should be my unit, the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of the MUP of Serbia, Belgrade, date such and such a date. And then after that there is the addressee, who the report is sent to, and the upper left-hand corner should contain the date on which this report was sent and also when it was received at the Ministry of the Interior. If this is the original, it could only have been produced without this heading at -- somewhere towards the end of the war when the ministry service, which is in charge of receiving documents, did not operate any longer and that Mr. Djordjevic requested a report. Because I previously noted that reports about the incident in Podujevo were also written by Mr. Simovic, as the commander of the Belgrade SAJ, and Mr. Stalevic, as the commander of the Pristina SAJ, as they were two directly superior officers who were there at the time when the incident happened. And it was also requested of me as the SAJ commander to write a report, regardless of the fact that I had not been there when this unfortunate incident occurred. But it's possible that someone asked Mr. Djordjevic that I also write a report, otherwise I cannot see why there shouldn't be a stamp from the registry of the MUP and that one cannot see the date when the report was made. I can just assume that it was at the end of the war when all the regular services at the Ministry of the Interior did not fully operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the third paragraph there dealing with the first engagement of the unit, are the statements made in that paragraph correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the document, the last page in English, the penultimate page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could read the last paragraph of that page and --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It indicates that: "A need again arose for the engagement of reservists so at the proposal of the SAJ commander Zivko Trajkovic and with the approval of the staff at Pristina and the chief of the department, 108 reservists were engaged under the leadership of Slobodan Medic." You wrote that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's -- those statements are correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In this report I did not write what I just stated, Your Honours, and it was that before the re-engagement of this combat group we talked on the issue of what should be done in case this unit was re-engaged. And that was why I as the commander, so that the report had some form, probably had to write that the unit would be re-engaged on my proposal because no one, even if it's the head of a department, could say, "I'm sending you a hundred members and you should see what you're going to do with them." So in order that this report would have an appropriate form, it says: "... at the proposal of the ... commander ... and with the approval of the staff in Pristina and the chief of the department ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Were any of the men that are alleged to have been involved in the shooting of the civilians at Podujevo a part of the group that was sent back?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The information that we had in the beginning - and this was a tacit agreement among the members of the group, that the responsibility for what had happened should be borne by the men who were marked as the perpetrators at that time - this information was what was available until one or two years after all the events in Kosovo. And only later on, at a later time, it became known that it was not the same number that was investigated immediately after the event and during the year after that, but that the number of perpetrators was actually greater and that some of the men who had been investigated had confessed and stated the whole truth. So if any of the members of this combat groups were included again in the composition of the group that was down there again for the second time, it was only for this reason and no other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your answer is not entirely clear at the end there. Can I just ask you the question again. Can you say whether or not you know if any of the men who were alleged to be involved in the shooting were re-engaged or sent back?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you ask me whether I know this now or if I knew that a year or two ago, then I would say yes. But if you ask me whether I knew that at the time when the combat group was re-engaged then my answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Mr. Milanovic, Mr. Milan Milanovic, and yourself met in Belgrade with Mr. Djordjevic to discuss the re-engagement. For how long had you known Mr. Milanovic? When did you first get to know him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Milanovic since September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What position did he occupy? And when I say "position," I mean professional or political position did he occupy at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: -- or during the period of the unit's engagement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, towards the end of that year and in early 1992, he was the assistant minister of defence in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at the end of 1991, what position did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1991 when the TO commander for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Mr. Radovan Stojicic was assigned to the position of assistant minister with the Ministry of the Interior in the Republic of Serbia, I was appointed the commander of the Territorial Defence for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think the then-Minister of Defence, Mr. Ilija Kojic. I don't recall precisely. It was either Ilija Kojic or Mr. Milan Milanovic, who was his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall who signed the instrument of your appointment at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At that time did you -- or let me put it this way: When did you first get to meet Mr. Medic, who was the leader of this group?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: When I met Mr. Medic for the first time he was not a leader of any group. I'm quite positive that we met either in Erdut or in Borovo, but at that time he was with the Territorial Defence of the so-called Sector South, which was the area from Vukovar towards the south. If you're asking me when I met him as the commander of that unit, because at that time I still think it was not an official unit, then I -- my answer is that it was in the course of 1992, around mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Do you know if Mr. Milanovic played any role in the formation of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Milanovic's task concerning that unit, given his position as the assistant minister for people's defence, was to assist in material and equipment. He was supposed to secure vehicles, uniforms, and facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999 at the time when they were engaged and incorporated into the SAJ, do you know if Mr. Mrgud played any role in that initial incorporation -- sorry, if Mr. Milanovic played any role in that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was in contact with Mr. Medic. I don't know whether Mr. Medic initiated that contact or whether he initiated contact with Mr. Medic. In any case, it seems that Mr. Milanovic was allowed to form a combat group so that that group could assist in the defence of the country, i.e., to assist in the defence of Kosovo and Metohija. When there were subsequent discussions about groups joining the SAJ, he conveyed that fact to Mr. Djordjevic, and that is how it came about that that combat group was engaged through the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and its reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999 do you know what position Mr. Milanovic held?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 Mr. Milanovic did not have a position in Serbia at least, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated to us earlier that when you discussed with Mr. Djordjevic the disarming of the unit, you requested that Mr. Medic accompany you to Prolom Banja to deal with that. Is there any particular reason why you would need Mr. Medic to -- to assist you in that regard? Could they have been disarmed by any of the commanders who were in the area at that time? I ask you the question because I think you indicated that at that time you were still recovering, and yet it was seen -- it was required that you go and do it and you needed to engage the assistance of Mr. Medic to disarm them -- sorry, Mr. Milanovic to disarm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I should rephrase that question entirely, Your Honour, because I started with the wrong name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why would you need, firstly, for you in your injured state to go to disarm them, and why would you need the assistance of Mr. Milanovic to go to disarm them, instead of having one of the MUP commanders within the chain of command do so?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that as a moral obligation on my part, to see that job concluded. I realised that Mr. Djordjevic had full confidence in me at that point in time. He believed I could perform that task, although I was still convalescing, and Mr. Milanovic was on good terms with Mr. Medic. Another reason was so that I don't go there completely alone to round off that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could one of the commanders on the ground, Mr. Stalevic or Mr. Simovic, disarm them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: They probably could, but, to repeat, I believed that that point in time I enjoyed Mr. Djordjevic's full confidence. He believed that I was the best person to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on, Mr. Trajkovic, to a different topic -- but before we do that could I ask you to explain one thing. I think you told us earlier that in respect to the Skorpions Mr. Djordjevic told you that these men were experienced or nearly experienced men, and later on you indicated to us -- please excuse me, I'm sorry. I think I'll rephrase that. You told us that when you were discussing the engagement with Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Djordjevic indicated that these were experienced or semi-experienced men who had been engaged in combat in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And I think later on you told us that when you checked it out only 15 to 16 of the men were from that earlier unit and the remainder had been mustered or engaged later on. Can you elaborate a little bit on that to explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: It is probable that Mr. Djordjevic had that piece of information about that group because of their commander. Those 15 or 16 guys who were with him had previously been with the Skorpions as the unit which served some time in Western Slavonia, and that is, I believe, the reason why he believed that that was a trained unit. Given the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the situation had been the same as it was in 1999, then there would not have been any problems. But at that early time any experienced soldier or fighter was more than welcome to join our units in order for us to be able to complete the tasks. And I believe there were good reasons at the time for which we needed that type of group and that type of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did Mr. Djordjevic share this -- well, let's move on. I withdraw that question. Are you aware - and I believe you are - that sometime in 2001 it became public that over 800 persons had been buried in clandestine graves at your Belgrade unit's headquarters in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I missed the year, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In around -- in 2001 there was a discovery, and it became a notorious issue in the media. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this -- the bodies were found at the SAJ base at the 13th of May centre in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at any time participate in any operation or any part of any operation to transport and conceal these -- remains of these people at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in any transport. If we are talking about concealing the fact, then my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just asking you now about the transport as well as the burial in the graves, the concealed graves there. Did you participate in that at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And when was the first time that you heard about the operation to transport bodies to and bury them at graves at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard about this situation was during a burial of one of our members in the territory of Belgrade. I don't know whether this was a memorial service or a funeral. In any case, it was in mid-April as far as I recall. It was the then-chief of the centre who remained behind with a small group of SAJ men to secure the centre at Batajnica who told me that at the centre, at Batajnica, on several occasions there were shipments of corpses who were then buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had -- I didn't realise the time was moving so quickly, and we are beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now, and we continue tomorrow at 2.15. A court officer will just confirm the arrangement, Mr. Trajkovic, with you this evening so that you know, but we will continue your evidence tomorrow at 2.15. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.08 p.m.,
